paper.title: Sibling Spillovers
paper.journal: NBER Working Paper Series, Working Paper No. 23062
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project number are given. …

registers.role: sample frame; birth outcomes (birth weight, five-minute APGAR score); exact date of birth and birth order; linkage of children to parents and siblings
treatment: the third child's disability status, and inpatient, outpatient and emergency room admissions of the third-born child by age five
outcome: cohort-standardized 9th grade exit exam grade point average
controls and mechanism variables: parental age, educational attainment, labor market status, earnings, leave taking, immigrant status, municipality of residence, family structure
sample frame; birth outcomes; paternity and marital status on the birth certificate

registers.name_in_paper: Florida school records (Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test)
registers.role: outcome: FCAT test scores in grades 3-8; treatment: disability categorization at kindergarten entry

linkages: Denmark: a unique personal identification number links generations, so children can be linked to their parents and siblings; birth records are matched to data from various administrative registers
Denmark: families are linked to the maternal grandmother's municipality of residence at the time of the third birth
Florida: the state's education and health agencies matched children along three dimensions -- first and last names, date of birth, and social security number
Florida: siblings are matched within a large majority of Florida counties

sample.universe: All singletons born in Florida between 1994 and 2002 and subsequently educated in Florida public schools, and all births in Denmark between 1990 and 2001 (selected from the Danish Birth Register's 1960-2010 coverage)
sample.unit_of_observation: child (first- and second-born children, nested within families; the comparison is within family across birth order)
selection_rules: Observe the first several births in a family
Restrict to families for whom the father is the same for the first two births
Exclude families where either of the first two children has an 'absent father' (paternity not claimed on the birth certificate)
Restrict to families with three or more children (Florida) / where the first three children are observed (Denmark)
Florida: children must be educated in Florida public schools and observed in grades 3-8
Denmark: children must be observed taking the 9th grade exit exam
sample.n_observations: 104,130 children (Florida, test scores); 57,162 children (Denmark, 9th grade GPA); 19,624 (Florida birth outcomes); 51,940 (Denmark birth outcomes)
sample.n_individuals: 9,812 Florida families and 28,581 Danish families in the main estimation samples; 80,879 Florida families with the first two children observed, of which 9,987 with three or more children; 134,277 Danish families with the first two children observed, of which 28,581 with the first three observed; 2,483 Florida and 4,430 Danish three-child families have a disabled third child observed by age five

construction_notes: Outcomes are normalized to have mean zero and standard deviation one; the Florida outcome combines math and reading assessments and pools a child's FCAT observations across grades to reduce measurement error
Danish outcome is the cohort-standardized 9th grade exit exam GPA, based on assessments by the student's teacher and by an external reviewer
Disability is measured on the school records in Florida (categorization at kindergarten entry, around age five) and in the medical registries in Denmark

Most common Florida disabilities observed by age five: speech impairment (48%), developmental delay (21%), language impairment (17%); most common Danish disabilities observed by age five: asthma (41%), congenital malformations and deformations of the musculoskeletal system (20%), congenital malformations of the circulatory system (10%)

The alternative treatment in Table 5 is defined from indicators recorded on the birth certificate: congenital anomaly, or abnormal condition at birth, or birth weight below 2500 grams, or gestational age below 37 weeks, or five-minute Apgar score below 6
Maternal education is coded as the level of maternal education at the time of the first sibling's birth
'Absent fathers' are cases in which paternity is not claimed on the birth certificate
Low birth weight is defined as birth weight less than 2500 grams; five-minute APGAR scores are observed on a ten-point scale

The grandmother in Table A2 is the mother of the child's mother; only families where the grandmother is not dead at the time of the third birth are considered, and grandparental living status is assigned based on the third birth
Table A3 columns (2)-(4) are cumulative DKK amounts from one to five years after the birth of the third child; columns (5)-(7) are counts of events by age five
Standard errors in the family-fixed-effects models are adjusted for clustering at the family level

links.pointer_quote: The magnitude of these differences is not trivial, for example, in Florida it is about half of the effect size the extra year of maternal education has on children's test scores.

claims.statement: In Florida, second-born children score lower on grades 3-8 standardized tests than their first-born siblings when the third-born child in the family is observed disabled by age five, relative to families whose third-born child is not.

treatment.label: 3rd observed disabled by age 5 (differential exposure to a disabled younger sibling)

register_source.value: Florida school records (disability categorization at kindergarten entry, Florida Department of Education)

definition.value: The coefficient β2 on the interaction D_f × M_if in equation (1): D = 1 if the family's third-born child is observed disabled by age five (school records at kindergarten entry in Florida; medical registries in Denmark), 0 otherwise; M = 1 if the child is second born (‘more exposed’) and 0 if first born (‘less exposed’). D itself is absorbed by the family fixed effect.

timing.value: Third child's disability observed by age five; the exposure difference accrues during the first- and second-born children's early childhood.

outcome.label: Test scores (standardized FCAT score, math and reading combined)

register_source.value: Florida Department of Education school records (Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test)

definition.value: Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test (FCAT) scores, administered in grades 3-8, pooled across grades, math and reading assessments combined, normalized to have mean zero and standard deviation one.

timing.value: Grades 3-8 (third through eighth grade), i.e. after the third sibling's birth.

units.value: standard deviations of the cohort-standardized test score distribution

estimand.target_population: Second-born children relative to their first-born siblings in three-plus-child families whose third-born child is observed disabled by age five
estimand.time_horizon: test scores measured in grades 3-8, i.e. in the older siblings' elementary and secondary schooling, after the third child's birth

population.description: First- and second-born children in Florida families with three or more children in which the father on the birth certificate is the same for the first two children
population.birth_cohorts: children born in Florida between 1994 and 2002
population.ages: grades 3-8 at the time the outcome is measured
population.selection: All singletons born in Florida 1994-2002 and subsequently educated in Florida public schools; families restricted to those with three or more children observed, with the same father on the birth certificate for the first two children; families in which either of the first two children has an absent father (paternity not claimed) are excluded.

identification.source_of_variation: Birth order within the family determines how much of early childhood a child spends with the third-born sibling; the first- versus second-born gap is compared across families whose third-born child is observed disabled by age five and families whose third-born child is not.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trends: in the absence of the third child's disability there would have been no differential trend in outcomes between first- and second-born children in families with and without a disabled third child.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Birth weight, log birth weight, low birth weight and five-minute APGAR scores used as placebo outcomes (Table 4, Table A1); placebo test on whether the second-born is identified as disabled by age five when second-to-third birth spacing is at least five years; differences in zip-code median income, first grade school quality, parental marriage/cohabitation and parental income.

key_assumptions.assumption: The third child's observed disability is not endogenously determined by the older siblings' outcomes (no reverse causation through increased parental or school vigilance triggered by a poorly performing second-born).
key_assumptions.supported_by: An alternative treatment defined by the third-born's problems recorded at birth (Table 5); models estimated on families in which neither the first- nor the second-born child is observed as disabled.

heterogeneity.dimension: Type of the third child's disability
heterogeneity.finding: The largest deleterious effects are found for physical disabilities (-0.077, standard error 0.027) rather than cognitive or behavioral disabilities (0.012, 0.040).

heterogeneity.dimension: Timing of the third child's disability
heterogeneity.finding: Effects are concentrated among disabilities observed early (by age five); the differential for disabilities first observed between ages five and ten is small and insignificant.

heterogeneity.dimension: Maternal education
heterogeneity.finding: A U-shaped pattern in Florida, with the most negative estimated spillovers at the top and the bottom of the SES distribution; equality across SES groups cannot be rejected (p = 0.45).

heterogeneity.dimension: Parental status of the third child (Florida)
heterogeneity.finding: Results are concentrated in families where the third child's father is different or absent.

heterogeneity.dimension: Immigrant status of the mother
heterogeneity.finding: Estimates are more negative, though not statistically significantly so, for immigrant mothers (-0.066, standard error 0.066) than for native-born mothers (-0.042, 0.024).

heterogeneity.dimension: Test subject
heterogeneity.finding: Larger estimates for reading than for mathematics (no coefficients reported).

key_assumptions.assumption: The third child's observed disability is not endogenously determined by the older siblings' outcomes (no reverse causation through increased parental or school vigilance triggered by a poorly performing second-born).
key_assumptions.supported_by: An alternative treatment defined by the third-born's problems recorded at birth (Table 5); models estimated on families in which neither the first- nor the second-born child is observed as disabled.

register_source.value: Florida Department of Education school records (Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test)

definition.value: Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test (FCAT) scores, administered in grades 3-8, pooled across grades, math and reading assessments combined, normalized to have mean zero and standard deviation one.

timing.value: Grades 3-8 (third through eighth grade), i.e. after the third sibling's birth.

units.value: standard deviations of the test score distribution

estimand.target_population: Second-born children relative to their first-born siblings in three-plus-child families whose third-born child is observed disabled by age five

population.description: First- and second-born children in Florida families with three or more children in which the father on the birth certificate is the same for the first two children
population.birth_cohorts: children born in Florida between 1994 and 2002
population.ages: grades 3-8 at the time the outcome is measured
population.selection: All singletons born in Florida 1994-2002 and subsequently educated in Florida public schools; families restricted to those with three or more children observed, with the same father on the birth certificate for the first two children; families in which either of the first two children has an absent father (paternity not claimed) are excluded.

identification.source_of_variation: Birth order within the family determines how much of early childhood a child spends with the third-born sibling; the first- versus second-born gap is compared across families whose third-born child is observed disabled by age five and families whose third-born child is not.

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trends: in the absence of the third child's disability there would have been no differential trend in outcomes between first- and second-born children in families with and without a disabled third child.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Birth weight, log birth weight, low birth weight and five-minute APGAR scores used as placebo outcomes (Table 4, Table A1); placebo test on whether the second-born is identified as disabled by age five when second-to-third birth spacing is at least five years; differences in zip-code median income, first grade school quality, parental marriage/cohabitation and parental income.

key_assumptions.assumption: The third child's observed disability is not endogenously determined by the older siblings' outcomes (no reverse causation through increased parental or school vigilance triggered by a poorly performing second-born).
key_assumptions.supported_by: An alternative treatment defined by the third-born's problems recorded at birth (Table 5); models estimated on families in which neither the first- nor the second-born child is observed as disabled.
